text: High above the clouds, among the towering peaks of an ancient mountain range, lives one of nature's most formidable predators.
The griffin.
With the powerful body of a lion and the wings and talons of an eagle, an adult griffin is capable of bringing down prey several times its own size.
But even the fiercest creatures must begin life somewhere.
Hidden within a nest perched high above the valley, a young griffin has recently emerged from its egg.
Covered in soft downy feathers, with oversized paws and wings far too small for flight, the chick bears little resemblance to the terrifying predator it will one day become.
For now, it is entirely dependent on its parents.
Each morning, the adults return from the hunt, carrying fresh meat to their hungry offspring.
The chick's hooked beak is already remarkably sharp, allowing it to tear small pieces of flesh, while its rapidly developing talons help it grip the rocky nest.
But growing up in the mountains is no easy task.
As the young griffin begins to explore, its curiosity frequently exceeds its coordination.
Its first attempts at flapping its wings are little more than clumsy leaps.
And a single misstep could send it plunging hundreds of metres into the valley below.
Fortunately, its mother is never far away.
For nearly a year, the young griffin remains under the protection of its parents, gradually developing the muscular chest and enormous flight feathers required to take to the skies.
Its eyesight becomes extraordinarily acute, allowing it to detect movement across vast distances.
Meanwhile, its once-soft paws develop into powerful weapons, equipped with curved claws capable of gripping struggling prey.
Eventually, the time comes for its first flight.
With an uncertain leap from the cliff's edge, the young griffin spreads its wings.
For a moment, it falls.
But then, catching the rising mountain winds, it begins to soar.
The helpless chick has taken its first step toward becoming one of the sky's most feared hunters.
And one day, it too will return to these mountains.
Not as a fledgling.
But as a guardian of the next generation.
